results.title: Intersting
results.text: An interesting introduction to many local customs - bring a Guide if you can to help get the most out of your visit

results.title: Eye opener
results.text: This was an interesting place to see. In the mornings the hindu's cremate their dead in the open for everyone to see. I found this interesting the process.

results.title: A must see
results.text: The best advice I can give about this most sacred of Hindu temples is to hire an official guide at the entrance to the site. You can hire one for around 200nrp pp and great value and very informative. BE WARNED. Cremations are carried out here constantly. Show respect and try to avoid taking pics of the funerals. Watch out for fake Sadhu's demanding money for pics.

results.title: Special place to visit for everyone
results.text:
Pashupatinath is an important Hindu temple in Kathmandu, dedicated to Shiva.

You have to pay an entrance fee of 500 rupees per person, knowing you can't visit the temples (only allowed for Hindu-people). You'll certainly will be approached by young Hindu "guides" who will try to sell you a guided tour. We firstly didn't want this tour, but then decided to agree for a small fee because it was a young student who spoke perfect English and didn't push us to take the tour. 

And in fact, it was very good. We got a lot more information than mentioned in the travel guides and were informed about the cremation ceremonies who take place around the clock on the river banks. 

So certainly a place you should visit when you are in Kathmandu and yes, a guide (if you feel comfortable with the youngster who approaches you) is recommended.

results.title: A must see place near Kathmandu
results.text: It is situated at the Bagmati river, the second holiest river to Ganges. First of all it is a very important place both for hindu and budist people. Unfortunately not hindus are not allowed on the main temple, but you can enjoy the view from the rivrside to people on the other side, in the temple. And you can visit small Shiva temples on the open riverbank - each is housing a lingam, a fertility symbol. And you can see how people are embarked to their last journey in fire. The only problem there are very insistive street salesmen/women who cannot let go of you without making a purchase. It is advisable to stay firm and refuse to buy anything otherwise you will be surrounded by a crowd of them.

results.title: Very atmospheric
results.text: Full of character, strange for westerners to see bodies being publicly cremated - can feel very uncomfortable but intriguing.  Colourful and great for photographs of the brightly dressed holy men and the dozens of monkeys.

results.title: Amazing Hundu temple complex
results.text: There really is no place else on earth like this; a must visit site.

results.title: A very spiritual place
results.text: I was allowed to go into the temple being a Hindu and it was an immensely spiritual experience. This was one of my highlights on my trip to Nepal

results.title: exotic but obnoxious
results.text: Being one of Unesco's world heritage in Kahtmandu, Pashupatinah keeps being exotic all the way through although lots of guts are needed to walk by the river lingered in a dreadful stench. Better get a mask just in case. More than dreadful, i should say deadful, since they cremate the dead people on the benches of the river. All a show. At the entrance, dozens of people will try to sell you necklaces, bags, rings, etc and will follow you until they succeed. Bargaining is mandatory. Gurus, women dressed with saris, monkeys, dogs and a troop of tourists intertwine in this particular place.

results.title: If in town you should visit this
results.text: Worth a visit. Get a guide (200 rupee) to tell you about the tempels and about the ceremonial burning. Entrance fee is 500 rupee.

results.title: House of gods a midst culture
results.text:
Pashupatinath is one of the most visited places in Kathmandu with over hundred thousand visitors showing their presence here. Pashupatinath is the holiest of all temples for Hindus.

Different shades of lives can be observed here. With Rishis and Shadhus (hermits and worshippers) chanting prayers to playful monkeys in the vicinity. Pashupatinath is also considered to be the holiest place for cremation for Hindus.

River Bagmati flows aside the temple. It is said that the river used to carry crystal clear water back in 1960s but sadly at present water is impure and unhealthy. It is also believed that water holds power of gods and washes away all sins and sorrows. 

Sounds, lights, people and exquisite experience of Nepali traditional culture, Hindu god worshiping and a warm feeling of being closer to gods is what Pashupatinath offers during a visit.

results.title: Excellent world heritage site
results.text:
We decided to get a guide for this area and we were not disappointed, he was a student but was full of the history and knowledge of this site, it  cost us 500 rupees, the entrance fee was 500 rupees per person too.  During our visit two cremations were taking place and it was fascinating to hear all about the cremations and the rituals of the family of the deceased.

Watch out for the holy men... our guide said you can give however much you wanted to have your picture taken but then one of them said after we had had our pictures taken that it was 100 rupees per holy man and in our case that was 500 rupees as there were 5 of them... needless to say we took plenty more photos to get our monies worth!

This is a must visit site when your in Kathmandu.

results.title: Fascinating, yet sombre, cultural highlight
results.text:
We visited Pashupatinath (Temple of Living Beings) on our second first morning in Kathmandu.  This was by far the highlight of our trip to Nepal.  Though some people may find the thought of watching cremations disturbing, we found it to be culturally insightful.  Non-Hindus are not permitted into the main temple, though there is plenty to see at spots that are accessible.  We wandered around the complex for a good portion of the morning, before taking a seat in the shade across the river from the main funeral pyres.  We watched from a distance as three bodies were washed, carried to the yak-butter covered stacked wood and then set alight.  We then watched the process by which the wood, with the body, is burned down to ashes, following which the entire burning pile is pushed into the river.  We then walked across the bridge to be closer to the funeral pyres, and watched as one deceased lady was laid to rest on the wood while her family removed her gold and other items.

The smell from the burning bodies is not so bad, though you can hear the body sizzle as you would if you were at a BBQ.  It is a good idea, especially if you are standing reasonably close to the funeral pyres, to carry a handkerchief to shield your nose and mouth.  If there is a wind the ashes are blown in all directions and you certainly want to try and avoid getting ashes in your lungs.

If you really want an insight into life in its purest form then you must visit Pashupatinath – for a most fascinating cultural insight the entrance fee of Rs 500 (around USD 6.80) per person is well worth it.  This is real life – this is not a site staged for tourists – it may not be suitable for children, unless they are mature enough to understand what is going on, and it certainly is not a place for people for whom the thought of death is disturbing.  With that having been said, I repeat what I said in my opening line – this was by far the highlight of our trip to Nepal, presenting an interesting yet somber insight into a culture that has existed for thousands of years.

results.title: Nice Temple
results.text: The temple is very nice, it has very significant value in Hindu religion, it is one of the great place to visit, only Hindu's are allowed to visit this temple, Non-Hindu Tourists can view it from outside only.

results.title: Spiritual bliss.....
results.text:
One should visit the Pashupatinath Temple while in Kathmandu. The temple is near the airport but once you take the lane towards the temple, its very very quiet. You can feel the calm and the energy surrounding the temple...
Camera's, mobiles and leather products are not allowd inside the temple-so make sure you dont carry it-there is a private shop just outside the temple where you can rent a locker for the visit duration....
You can buy offerings (optional) for the temple at 300 Nepali Rupees. Many touts and guides are awaiting outside the temple-choose prudently, maybe a older person as guide is better option. 
The priests inside will expect a dakshina (optional) for their services-you may use your discretion. 50 to 100 nepali rupees is ok. More is upto you....
A good place where you can deposit the shoes in bags is also available within the temple premises just before you enter the main temple gate so do not deposit or leave your shoes way outside the temple.
527 Shivalingams are there which are supposedly to be in existance since 13 century-it is said all sins of  last lives are forgiven if you walk through the lanes of the Shivalingams...
Donations are an optional effect. You may donate at the donation boxes rather than handling out cash.....

results.title: Don't miss this
results.text: This place is so interesting as it is where they do the cremations.  Going with a guide is not a bad idea since they can explain what is going on.  Plan on staying there a while so you can see the ceremonies (2 hours or so).

results.title: must visit
results.text:
this place is a must see for all tourists. You'll probably spend a couple of hours here. Be smart in using your camera...
Dont pay more then Rs. 250 for a taxi from Thamel.

results.title: NOT A TOURIST ATTRACTION...THIS IS THE REAL THING!!!
results.text:
since 2008, during three trips to nepal, i've visited
pashupatinath on many occasions, the most recent
being march 2011, the day before the birthday of 
'shiva.'  if you enjoy photography...without doubt,
this is your place.  one could spend hours here,
seeing the cycle of life take place right in front of 
you.  hindu belief is that as soon as possible after 
death, the physlcal body should be burned, so that
the spirit may be freed.  this ritual goes on around
the clock here.  families gather to say goodbye to 
the deceased, while the body is prepared for 
cremation...part of this may include many family 
members taking photos of the deceased with cell
phone cameras...  during this time, a priest from 
the temple prepares a funeral pyre on the other 
side of the complex.  the body is wrapped in cloth, 
carried to the pyre, and then around it three times.
often, foods are left near the body to accompany the 
deceased on their journey.  family often have to 
fight-off pesky monkeys, who want their share of 
the fruit.  the eldest son, often dressed in white, 
the color of mourning, will light the fire...and
the family sits peacefully, while the body is 
consumed.  whatever is left, is swept into the 
river, where young boys then plunge in to 
recover anything that could be sold for a few 
rupees.   there is nothing gross or gruesome 
about this...it's just death, another part of life...
as it's dealt with by another culture.  in fact, it's
just another page in your book of education.
     if you conduct yourself with respect, you 
may take photos from across the river.  
unlike in veranasi, india...you're not beseiged 
for unreasonable sums of money.  a telephoto 
lens of reasonable length will get you as close 
as you'd want to get.  it seems as though most 
are here to pay respect to the dead, and to pray, 
rather than to scam tourists... in veranasi...we
were asked for 1,000 inr ($25usd), for one
photo...better to come to pashupatinath.
     also in the area, are 'sadhus' or hindu 
holy men...some of them are real characters, 
and very worthy of your photographic efforts.  
they'll expect money...so you should go to 
pashupatinath with lots of small bills...20 
and 50 rupees...for this purpose.  see the 
attached photos.  if you visit from year to 
year...you'll see the same guys... this year 
i brought same photo prints...they were
fascinated.
      there are guides available near the 
entrance on the airport road...i've never 
hired one, as i always move about with 
nepali friends.  either can help you run 
the gauntlet of semi-agressive
vendors near the entrance.  the entry 
fee is modest...whatever it is...it's well 
worth it.

results.title: Be prepared for burning bodies.
results.text: Really interesting. People throw coins and statues in with loved ones.  The kids sift through water full of human ashes for items to sell. No one minds. which i thought would be disrespectful.  Go down to where they are. Tell will pay per item. Dont pay at end or you will get kids swarming you.

results.title: A definite "must see" if you're in Nepal!"
results.text: The day we arrived as we crossed the river our host pointed out the fact that creamations were taking place.  It was definitely not something I had expected to hear or much less be able to observe while in Nepal.  But of everything we saw, this was probably the most intriguing.  It very difficult to put it into words but it overwhelms your senses.  Even emotionally, it's very overwhelming-if you're planning to visit Kathmandu, I would definitely recommend you visit this site-even spring for the few rupees to have a guide explain everything as you go through!
